topic.title: Open to work, because of AI
topic.claim: Housing.com and IBM cutting jobs the same day, both filed under a year of AI-cited layoffs, says more about convenient corporate language than about AI.
topic.behaviour: Housing.com laid off around 300 employees and IBM cut 100 roles in Ahmedabad on the same day, part of a year where Indian startup layoffs crossed 4,500 across eight months, including Livspace cutting nearly 1,000 jobs (12% of staff) as part of what it called 'AI-native' restructuring.
topic.mechanism: Saying 'AI is restructuring us' reads better on LinkedIn than saying 'we needed to cut costs', so the stated reason for a layoff and the actual reason aren't always the same thing.
topic.group: 20-something professionals in product, HR and ops roles at startups

sources.excerpt: Housing.com laid off 300 employees on Oct 1, 2026 in India. This represented 60% of their workforce. IBM conducted layoffs of 100 employees on Oct 1, 2026 in Ahmedabad, India. The reduction affected their tech and cloud services divisions. Both announcements were categorized as rumored at the time of reporting.

sources.fact: Indian startups cut more than 4,500 jobs over eight months per Longhouse Consulting data, with Livspace laying off around 1,000 employees as part of an AI-driven cost rationalisation.
sources.excerpt: Indian startups have cut more than 4,500 jobs over the past eight months. Data cited by The Times of India from executive search firm Longhouse Consulting. Home décor platform Livspace recently laid off around 1,000 employees as part of an AI-driven cost rationalisation effort. The restructuring was described by the company as 'operational streamlining rather than wholesale replacement of roles,' though it was characterized as an 'AI-driven' initiative by the reporting source.

sources.fact: More than 4,500 professionals have been laid off across Indian startups since July, with Livspace cutting 1,000 jobs framed as an AI-focused strategy.
sources.excerpt: More than 4,500 professionals laid off since July last year. Data from Longhouse Consulting indicates that the surge in job cuts is the result of regulatory changes, investor pressure for profitability and a rapid pivot towards artificial intelligence-driven business models. Livspace recently reduced its workforce by 1,000 employees as part of an AI-focused strategy, highlighting how automation is replacing traditional roles.

paragraphs: Housing.com cut around 300 people and IBM cut 100 in Ahmedabad on the same day, and both got quietly filed under the same story everyone's telling this year: AI is restructuring us.
No. Costs are restructuring you. AI is just the word that sounds better on LinkedIn.
Swipe to read →
Look at the year. Indian startup layoffs crossed 4,500 in eight months. Livspace let go of nearly 1,000 people in what reporters framed as AI-driven restructuring.
Notice the shift in language. Nobody says we overhired in 2021. Nobody says the funding dried up. They say AI, like a tool walked in on Monday and quietly did everyone's job over the weekend.

I've sat in enough meetings to know how a sentence gets chosen. A company can say two things about the same decision: that it needed to cut costs and these roles went first, or that it's becoming AI-native and reshaping the org.
Same 300 people walking out. But one version makes investors nervous and one makes you sound like you're ahead of the curve. Guess which one goes in the post.
This actually bothers me. The person laid off now has to carry that story too.

If the company says AI did it, then the ops or HR or product person at their desk starts wondering if they're the one the machine replaced. It's not about their work anymore. It's about a word a leadership team picked because it reads cleaner.
And it's a very convenient word. AI takes no blame. You can't be angry at a cost-cutting spreadsheet the way you can be angry at a model that supposedly got smart overnight.

You can announce that automation replaced a role long before any automation actually does it. But 'automation replaced the role' closes the conversation faster than 'the numbers didn't work', so that's the one they reach for.
I'm saying the stated reason and the real reason are rarely the same sentence, and this year they've drifted further apart than usual.
So when you read the next layoff dressed up as a strategy, separate the two. Ask what the number was and ask what the headline was.

topic.title: Fresher Hiring In IT Just Collapsed 80%
topic.claim: Fresher hiring in IT dropping roughly 80% from its peak this year is this generation finding out, in real time, that the safest career path their parents picked for them isn't safe anymore.
topic.behaviour: India's IT sector is shedding an estimated 25,000-35,000 jobs in 2026, with TeamLease reporting 10,000-15,000 silent layoffs by May and fresh cuts at Qualcomm and Oracle's India units, while TCS, Infosys and Wipro scale back graduate intake and over 12,700 techies who had moved abroad have returned this year.
topic.mechanism: Engineering into an IT job was the default safe bet for a generation of Indian families, and AI-driven restructuring is hitting exactly the entry-level, high-volume hiring that made that bet feel safe.
topic.group: Engineering graduates and early-career tech employees, and their parents

TeamLease reported 10,000-15,000 silent layoffs by May 2026
fresher hiring has collapsed roughly 80% from its peak
more than 12,700 Indian tech workers who had moved abroad have returned this year
topic.news_peg: 2026 IT layoff wave and fresher hiring collapse reported October 21, 2026
topic.why_now: Numbers published this week, campus and LinkedIn anxiety threads trending

sources.fact: Fresher hiring in India's IT sector has fallen roughly 80%, from a peak of 600,000 in FY22 to about 120,000 in FY25, per Xpheno, with Wipro and Infosys also trimming graduate intake targets.
sources.excerpt: Fresher hiring in India's IT sector has fallen from a peak of 600,000 in FY22 to about 120,000 in FY25, according to Xpheno, marking an 80% decline. Wipro has reduced its fresher hiring guidance to 7,500–8,000, from an earlier estimate of 10,000 and has onboarded roughly 5,000 so far. Infosys presents a relatively stronger outlook, maintaining its target of 20,000 fresher hires, with 18,000 already onboarded. Nearly 1,000 candidates are still awaiting joining letters from Tech Mahindra, while more than 200 Wipro recruits have flagged deferred onboarding. Hiring 10,000 freshers can require an outlay of around Rs 400 crore in salaries alone, excluding training costs.

sources.fact: On October 21, 2026, reports confirmed fresh Qualcomm layoffs affecting its large India engineering hubs, following Oracle's roughly 10,000 India job cuts, amid a wave of over 12,700 tech professionals returning from the US.
sources.excerpt: Qualcomm will cut jobs globally in a 'performance-focused reduction' following its annual employee reviews, per CEO Cristiano Amon's internal memo. The chipmaker stated that business priorities, organisational needs, skills and expertise would be considered in making the cuts. Notifications are slated to begin in November. Qualcomm runs large engineering centres in India — Hyderabad and Bengaluru are among its biggest global design hubs. Oracle eliminated approximately 10,000 Indian positions — representing one of its largest bases outside the United States. The company deployed terminations via email at 6 AM with immediate effect. Around 12,700 professionals had made the move [from US to India] by September 2026, raising competitive pressure domestically. Returning engineers now prioritize artificial intelligence, cloud computing, cybersecurity and product leadership skills. C-DAC opened roughly 844 Project Engineer and Project Associate posts across 11 centres with freshers eligible to apply before the October 26 deadline.

sources.fact: Around 12,700 Indian tech professionals had returned from the US to India by September 2026, per Xpheno data reported by The Economic Times, putting 2026 on track to surpass last year's record of 15,100 amid visa uncertainty and layoffs.
sources.excerpt: Around 12,700 professionals had made the move by September 2026, according to data from Xpheno, as reported by The Economic Times. This figure puts 2026 on track to surpass last year's record of 15,100, with numbers rising from 7,200 in 2023 to 9,800 in 2024. The exodus is attributed to growing uncertainty over immigration and visa policies under the Trump administration, combined with rising layoffs and limited stability in global hiring. The movement was also influenced by a suspension of PERM processing (Program Electronic Review Management) for major tech recruiters including Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys, Cognizant, Capgemini, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and Tata — a key step in employer-sponsored green card applications.

paragraphs: Engineering into an IT job was the safest bet an Indian family could make. Paper degree, campus placement, maybe an onsite stint, done. This year that bet is quietly coming apart. Fresher hiring in IT is down roughly 80% from its peak, and a whole generation is finding out that safe isn't safe anymore.
Swipe to read →
Look at the size of the drop. Fresher intake went from a peak of 600,000 in FY22 to about 120,000 in FY25, going by Xpheno. That's not a bad quarter, that's the whole floor moving.

This was the plan papa and chacha agreed on without a single argument. Science stream, B.Tech, a service company, a stable salary by 22. The one path in an Indian house that nobody debated at dinner, because everyone already knew it worked.
Wipro trimmed its fresher guidance to 7,500 to 8,000. Oracle cut around 10,000 India jobs, the terminations sent by email at 6 AM. Qualcomm is doing its own round.

And the ones still technically hired are stuck in the worst place. Nearly a thousand candidates at Tech Mahindra are waiting on joining letters, and over 200 Wipro recruits were told their onboarding is deferred. Not rejected, not working. Just a boy at home holding an offer that means nothing yet, telling relatives he's joining soon.

The exact thing that made this career feel safe is the thing killing it. It was safe because they hired in bulk, thousands of freshers for repetitive, entry-level work. That bulk is precisely what AI restructuring eats first. The safety was the vulnerability the whole time.
Meanwhile over 12,700 people who went abroad came back this year, loaded with AI and cloud skills, now competing for the same shrinking set of desks.

And the cruel bit is who has to absorb it. Not the parents who picked the path. The 22-year-old who scored the way he was told, cracked the placement, and still ended up explaining a gap year he didn't choose.

The parents aren't villains here. They optimised for the world they knew, where this degree meant a letter and a salary and an end to log kya kahenge. The map was right for thirty years. It just stopped matching the ground this year.

So the real shift isn't 25,000 to 35,000 jobs going in 2026. It's that the one career Indian families treated as risk-free has joined every other career as a bet. There is no lane left that you can point your kid at and stop thinking.
If you're a parent now, the honest thing is harder than the old plan. You can't hand a child one safe answer anymore.

topic.title: An ad got memed before the campaign even finished running
topic.claim: JioStar's Kohli-Rohit ad getting renamed 'Ro-Ko' by the internet within days of airing is the fastest I've seen a brand's own message get taken over by the audience's joke.
topic.behaviour: A JioStar ad featuring Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma spawned the nickname 'Ro-Ko', with fans remixing the ad's tone into meme formats about the duo's on-field partnership and off-field banter.
topic.mechanism: Cricket ads get adopted and remixed faster than any other category in India because the goodwill is already built in, the brand doesn't have to create affection, it just has to borrow it.
topic.group: cricket fans and marketers watching how fast campaigns get taken over

Nickname 'Ro-Ko' coined and spread by fans online

sources.fact: JioStar's new advertisement featuring Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli explicitly built its joke around the fan-coined 'Ro-Ko' nickname for the duo, released ahead of India's ODI series against Sri Lanka.
sources.excerpt: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli have turned the famous 'Ro-Ko' nickname into their own joke in a new JioStar advertisement ahead of India's upcoming ODI series against Sri Lanka. Rohit has often used the word 'who' while trying to remember or describe someone without taking their name directly, and this time Kohli uses the moment to have some fun with his teammate. The advertisement begins with Rohit and Kohli meeting again after some time. Rohit points out that it has been years, while Kohli reminds him that the fun is still the same. When Kohli says "our boys are also excited," Rohit responds with his famous 'woh', and Kohli plays along with the joke. The Indian batting icons mimicked team celebrations, including using sign language to help identify Ravindra Jadeja through his famous sword celebration, and mimicked Shubman Gill's familiar hat-doffing celebration.

sources.fact: JioStar officially released the Rohit Sharma-Virat Kohli ad film on 7 October 2026, confirming the news peg's timing for the campaign ahead of the 2027 World Cup.
sources.excerpt: The film was released on 7 October 2026. JioStar has unveiled a new film bringing together Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli in a rare and candid coming together, setting the stage for what promises to be a monumental year ahead for Team India. The film places the two in a light-hearted conversation as they reminisce about their journey with Team India. It celebrates their passion for the game and offers fans a glimpse of the duo's playful side, as they cheekily recreate the signature celebrations of KL Rahul, Ravindra Jadeja and captain Shubman Gill. Closing message: "Desh ka sawaal hai, maza toh aayega" (It's a matter of the country's pride, it's going to be fun).

sources.fact: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli themselves publicly acknowledged that 'Ro-Ko' had become a viral fan- and broadcaster-adopted tag that they found amusing, confirming the organic audience takeover of the nickname.
sources.excerpt: I think we were together. This started, I think, when we were playing in Australia, or right after Australia when we came to India. That's when this started, and whenever this plays on TV, we look at each other and laugh. Which is good, it's fun. People want masala, so there you go, there is some masala. Ro-Ko has a nice ring to it. It sounds nice, it sounds good, and people are having a lot of fun with it. Now that we only play one format, even from the broadcaster's perspective, I'm sure it's a very nice tagline to use - 'Oh, Ro-Ko aa gaye! They are back'.

paragraphs: JioStar put out a Rohit and Kohli ad this month, and within days everyone was calling it the Ro-Ko ad. Except fans didn't invent that nickname off the ad. They'd been calling the two Ro-Ko. The brand just picked up a joke already lying there.
Swipe to read →

The film dropped on 7 October. Rohit and Kohli meeting after a while, Kohli ribbing Rohit about his habit of saying woh instead of naming someone. They do sign language for Jadeja's sword celebration, copy Gill's hat tip, and sign off with *desh ka sawaal hai, maza toh aayega*. All timed before the Sri Lanka ODIs, with the 2027 World Cup sitting right there.

Then the internet did what it does, and the Ro-Ko tag was everywhere. Rohit himself said whenever it plays on TV they look at each other and laugh. People want masala, so there's your masala. Ro-Ko has a nice ring to it, he said.

Marketers quietly know this. A cricket ad doesn't have to make you feel anything. The feeling is already built. You've been watching these two most of your life, you have opinions about both, you've argued about them at every family lunch. The brand isn't creating that affection. It's renting it and putting its logo at the end.

In almost any other category, your campaign getting renamed by the audience is a small disaster. You spent weeks on a line and the internet tossed it for its own joke. Here it's the opposite. JioStar didn't lose the message to the Ro-Ko joke. It built the ad on top of a joke fans had already made, and let them carry it further.

The fastest way for a campaign to travel is to not fully own it. Give people something half-finished they can bend into their own version. Cricket gets this for free because the love is pre-loaded. Everyone else has to earn the affection first, then hope the audience even bothers to remix it.

The ad built its joke around the fan-coined 'Ro-Ko' nickname and was released ahead of India's ODI series against Sri Lanka, with Kohli teasing Rohit's habit of saying 'woh'.
In the ad the duo recreate team celebrations, including sign language for Ravindra Jadeja's sword celebration and Shubman Gill's hat-doffing, closing with 'Desh ka sawaal hai, maza toh aayega'.
Rohit Sharma said that whenever the Ro-Ko trend plays on TV they look at each other and laugh, that people want masala, and that 'Ro-Ko has a nice ring to it'.
The 'Ro-Ko' nickname was coined and spread by fans online.

topic.title: Nobody's Buying The iPhone In Cash Anymore
topic.claim: The iPhone 17 becoming India's best-selling phone isn't really an iPhone story, it's a credit story, people financing a month's salary through EMI while credit card spending hits ₹23.6 lakh crore like that's just how you buy things now.
topic.behaviour: iPhone 17 topped India's smartphone volume charts with over 4% market share, and during Big Billion Days prices dropped to ₹77,999-79,999 against the ₹99,900 MRP, driven heavily by no-cost EMI offers, while credit card spending hit a record ₹23.62 lakh crore in FY26, up nearly 12%, with monthly spends crossing ₹2 trillion for three straight months.
topic.mechanism: When EMI and credit cards make the sticker price invisible, people stop comparing the real cost of a purchase and start comparing the monthly number instead, and the monthly number always looks smaller than it is.
topic.group: Young professionals financing lifestyle and gadget purchases on EMI and credit cards

monthly credit card spends crossed ₹2 trillion for three straight months

sources.fact: India's total credit card spending hit a record ₹23.62 trillion in FY2026, up 11.98% year-on-year, with monthly spends crossing ₹2 trillion multiple times during the year.
sources.excerpt: FY2026 total credit card spend: ₹23.62 trillion, up 11.98% year-on-year from ₹21.09 trillion in FY2025. This represents a deceleration from the prior year's expansion rate of 15.5%. The report indicates that monthly spending exceeded ₹2 trillion on multiple occasions during the fiscal year. Specifically, the data shows four separate months in 2025-26 when spending crossed this threshold—a significant achievement compared to earlier periods when such peaks were infrequent. March 2026: ₹2.19 trillion (described as "a three-month high"). December 2025: ₹2.05 trillion. January 2026: ₹2.00 trillion. The article notes that "each time monthly spending dips sharply...the following month tends to rebound strongly," illustrating the seasonal volatility characteristic of India's credit card market.

sources.fact: The iPhone 17 drove Apple's best-ever sales month in India, accounting for 57% of all iPhones sold — the highest-ever adoption rate for a new iPhone generation in the country, per Counterpoint.
sources.excerpt: Counterpoint's projections showed that the iPhone 17 accounted for 57% of all iPhones sold—the highest-ever adoption rate of Apple's latest generation smartphone in India to date.

paragraphs: The iPhone 17 is India's best-selling phone right now. Over 4% of every phone sold.
That's not an Apple story. That's a credit story. Nobody paid ₹99,900. They paid ₹8,667 a month and told themselves that's different.
Swipe to read →
During Big Billion Days the iPhone 17 dropped from ₹99,900 to around ₹77,999 if you had the right bank card.
But the number that actually moved it wasn't the discount. It was the no-cost EMI. Six months, nine months, split it up, start at ₹8,667.
A phone that costs most people more than a month's salary suddenly reads like a Swiggy order you spread across a year.
This is the whole trick, and it works on everyone. The sticker price disappears and your brain only sees the monthly number.
₹8,667 feels fine. You can do ₹8,667. What's ₹8,667 next to a salary.
You never once add it up. Because the day you add it up, you're holding a phone that cost you a month of work, and nobody wants to feel that when they're paying.
And it's not just phones. Indians spent ₹23.62 lakh crore on credit cards last year, up almost 12%. Monthly spends crossed ₹2 trillion in four separate months this year.
12.16 crore cards in circulation now.
It means people got comfortable paying for today's thing with next month's money, one swipe at a time.
The funny part is nobody feels reckless doing it. No-cost EMI even sounds responsible. You're being smart. You're using the offer. You'd be a fool to pay upfront.
So the phone, the TV, the vacation, the kitchen appliance all become ₹8,667 a month. Twelve little numbers that each look harmless.
And then the 2nd of every month arrives and every one of them hits at once.
This is what the festive sale actually sells now. Not the discount. The permission to not think about the real price.
If you're building anything with a price tag in India, the real product isn't your product anymore. It's the monthly number you can make it shrink into.
The brand that wins this month isn't the one with the best phone. It's the one that made ₹99,900 feel like ₹8,667.

topic.title: Groceries Got Cheaper, Phones Didn't
topic.claim: GST 2.0 made shampoo and dal cheaper and crashed inflation to 0.25%, but the GST Council held mobile phones at 18%, and that tells you exactly which purchases the government still treats as a luxury.
topic.behaviour: CPI inflation fell to 0.25% in October 2026 as GST cuts on everyday items fed through, with food inflation at -5.02% and small cars and two-wheelers now taxed at 18% instead of 28%, while the GST Council's October 8 meeting kept mobile phones unchanged at 18%.

sources.fact: India's CPI inflation fell to 0.25% in October, with food inflation at -5.02%, largely due to the full month's impact of GST rate cuts.
sources.excerpt: India's inflation rate based on the Consumer Price Index (CPI) declined further to 0.25 per cent in October according to the Ministry of Statistics. food inflation fell deeper in the negative zone at (-) 5.02 per cent from (-) 2.28 per cent in September, marking the fifth consecutive month of negative food inflation. The decline in headline inflation and food inflation during October is mainly attributed to the full month's impact of the decline in GST along with favorable base effects and drops in prices for cooking oils, vegetables, fruits, and other items. The RBI Governor emphasized that the GST rate rationalisation would lead to a reduction in prices of several items in the CPI basket.

sources.fact: GST rate cuts on everyday items (vehicles, consumer goods) drove retail inflation down to a decade low of 0.25% in October, confirming the GST 2.0 CPI news peg.
sources.excerpt: The GST rate cuts brought down retail inflation by 85 basis points to a record low of 0.25 per cent in October, according to experts. The Consumer Price Index-based retail inflation was lowest in the current series (base year 2012), which captures data since January 2014. The new GST regime slashed the levy on entry-level two-wheelers and cars to 18% from 28% -- a move aimed at reviving demand in the price-sensitive segment. October's overall vehicle sales, the first full-month numbers since goods and services tax (GST) was simplified on September 22, jumped 40.5% year-on-year to more than 4.2 million units. Passenger vehicle sales rose 11.4%, while two-wheeler sales surged nearly 52%, both at record-high levels.

sources.fact: The 57th GST Council meeting on 8 October 2026 kept mobile phones unchanged at 18% GST despite industry requests for a cut to 5%.
sources.excerpt: The 57th GST Council meeting on 8 October 2026 made no change to the 18% GST on mobile phones. Phone GST has sat at 18% for six and a half years, unchanged since April 2020. Prior to this decision, the India Cellular and Electronics Association wrote to the finance minister on 2 September seeking a cut to 5%, but this request was not approved at the Council meeting.

paragraphs: Inflation fell to 0.25% in October, the lowest in a decade. And your phone, the thing you run your entire life on, is still taxed like a treat you don't really need.
Swipe to read →

GST 2.0's full month showed up in the numbers. Food inflation went deeper negative at -5.02%, the fifth month in a row. Cooking oil, vegetables, fruit, all down. Small cars and two-wheelers went from 28% tax to 18%, and two-wheeler sales jumped almost 52% in the first full month after. Cheaper stuff, people buy more. No mystery there.

Then the GST Council met on October 8. The phone industry had written in asking for the tax to come down to 5%. The Council kept it at 18%. That's where phones have sat since April 2020. Six and a half years, no movement, while everything around them got re-sorted and relabelled.

A tax slab isn't just a number. It's the government telling you what it thinks counts as a basic need. Dal, basic. A scooter, now basic. Your phone, still filed on the same shelf as the stuff you buy to show off.

Which is funny, because try getting through one normal day without it. Your salary lands there. Your rent goes out from there. UPI, the doctor's appointment, your boss's 9pm message, the bus ticket, the bank. The phone stopped being a gadget years ago. It's the counter where your whole life runs.

And it hits hardest the people who have the least room to spare. The delivery guy whose entire income lives inside an app. The woman running her shop off a QR code taped to the wall. For them the phone isn't a want, it's the job itself. The slab doesn't see any of that.

So when something gets held at the higher slab, read it as the government's quiet opinion of you. They decided the phone is something you want, not something you need. Everyone holding one for twelve hours a day already knows that's backwards.

topic.title: Gold Hit ₹1.5 Lakh And Nobody Stopped Buying It
topic.claim: Gold crossing ₹1,50,300 for 10 grams didn't kill the Dhanteras ritual this year, it just shrank it, everyone's still buying, just a lot less of it.
topic.behaviour: Urban buyers are switching to lightweight jewellery, small digital gold SIPs and gold ETFs instead of coins, and jewellers report footfall holding up even as grams purchased per customer falls sharply.
topic.mechanism: Buying gold at Dhanteras is a ritual obligation more than an investment call, so when the price spikes, people don't skip the ritual, they just downsize the quantity until the act of buying still happened.

sources.fact: Gold hit a fresh record of ₹1,50,300 per 10 grams in India on October 19, 2026, driven by festive demand ahead of Dussehra and Diwali.
sources.excerpt: Gold prices in the Indian market reached a fresh high of ₹1,50,300 per 10 grams on Monday. This represents a daily increase of ₹400. This increase is driven by high festive demand as India prepares for Dussehra and Diwali. ... seasonal wedding and festival demand within India serves as a primary price driver, with consumer buying has surged, pushing physical gold to trade at a premium during this period.

sources.fact: Ahead of the 2026 festive season, World Gold Council data shows jewellers' same-store sales rising on higher ticket sizes even as buyer/footfall growth stayed only mid-single digit, alongside strong growth in lightweight jewellery, digital gold and gold ETF demand.
sources.excerpt: Gold prices have remained rangebound in October. Seasonal demand is gathering pace as the market enters the key festive and wedding period. Retailers are emphasizing fresh designs and lighter weight pieces, which offer greater wearability, to attract consumers during peak purchasing periods. Digital gold demand remained firm in September, with purchases rising to INR25.9bn (US$271mn), up 4% from August and 83% higher than a year earlier; purchases totalled 16.3t year-to-date compared with 9.2t in the corresponding period of 2025, reflecting 76% growth. Gold ETFs saw stronger net inflows in September, reaching INR44.5bn (US$466.2mn), the highest in seven months, with momentum continuing into October. Same-store sales growth of around 20% was reported, while buyer growth remained in the mid-single digits, indicating higher average ticket sizes rather than increased customer volume.

sources.fact: Dhanteras 2026 falls on Friday, November 6, 2026, with bar-and-coin investment demand (lightweight, divisible gold formats) climbing to a record 52% share of India's total gold demand as jewellery demand softened under record prices.
sources.excerpt: This year, Dhanteras falls on Friday, November 6, 2026, the opening day of the five-day Diwali festival. By late January, spot gold had pushed past $5,300 an ounce for the first time in history, and domestic 24-karat gold touched somewhere between roughly ₹169,000 and ₹179,000 per 10 grams in the January to early March window, an all-time high for the Indian market. ... bar and coin investment already made up 52 percent of India's total domestic gold demand, the highest share on record since 2013, up from 42 percent a year earlier, even as jewelry demand softened.

paragraphs: Gold hit ₹1,50,300 for 10 grams in mid-October this year, and everyone assumed the ritual would quietly die.
It didn't. People are still walking into the shop. They're just walking out with a lot less.
Swipe to read →

Dhanteras is on November 6 this year, and buying gold that day was never really an investment decision. It's an obligation. You buy because papa bought, because his papa bought, because not buying feels like you're tempting something.
So when the price jumps, nobody sits down and calculates returns. They just buy the ritual-sized version of it.
That's exactly what jewellers are seeing. Footfall is holding up fine. The shop is full. But the grams per customer have dropped sharply.
Same number of people, much smaller purchases. The coin became a lighter coin. The necklace became a thin chain. The gift became a pendant you can barely feel in your hand.

You can see it in where the money is going. Lightweight jewellery everyone can wear, not store. Digital gold in tiny amounts on an app. Gold ETFs sitting in a demat account nobody at Diwali will ever see.
The buying didn't shrink. It just got divisible.
Nobody says it out loud. The gold was never fully about the gold.

It was about proving, once a year, that the family is doing okay. That we bought something. So when the price climbs to a record, you don't skip the proof, you just quietly reduce the quantity until the receipt still exists and the photo still happens.
This is the thing with Indians and anything that gets witnessed. The act matters more than the amount. A visible coin beats an invisible SIP every Dhanteras.

The jewellers already figured it out. Fresh designs, lighter pieces, bigger tickets. They're not selling you gold anymore. They're selling you the ability to keep the ritual going at whatever price the year hands you.
